name: Drug-Induced Liver Injury
pinyin: yào wù xìng gān sǔn shāng
preview_text: TCM doesn't just treat the liver enzyme number - it treats the pattern behind it. Whether your symptoms are jaundice with a bitter taste, or dull pain with dry eyes and night sweat...
conventional_description: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) occurs when a medication, herbal supplement, or other substance damages the liver. Symptoms range from mild, silent enzyme elevations to severe fatigue, jaundice, nausea, and right upper abdominal pain. Diagnosis relies on a careful medication history, blood tests showing elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin, and imaging to rule out other causes. In serious cases, the injury can progress to acute liver failure.
conventional_treatments: The cornerstone of Western management is immediately stopping the offending drug. For acetaminophen overdose, N-acetylcysteine is given to replenish glutathione. Otherwise, treatment is largely supportive - rest, hydration, and monitoring liver function until the organ heals on its own. Corticosteroids are sometimes used for severe immune-mediated reactions, and liver transplantation becomes the only option if the damage is irreversible.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees drug-induced liver injury as a form of toxic heat invading the body and lodging in the Liver. The Liver governs the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, and when that flow is disrupted by heat toxins, Qi stagnates - causing the distending, uncomfortable sensation under the ribs that so many patients describe.
At the same time, the toxins weaken the Spleen, the organ responsible for transforming food and fluids into usable energy. A compromised Spleen leads to dampness, fatigue, and loose stools, which is why digestive symptoms so often accompany liver injury.
Over time, that dampness can combine with heat to create a thick, greasy obstruction in the Liver and Gallbladder. This damp-heat pattern is what produces the classic signs of jaundice, dark urine, and a bitter taste in the mouth. In other cases, the stagnation becomes so severe that it blocks Blood flow, creating a fixed, stabbing pain that feels worse with pressure.
Meanwhile, the original toxic heat can slowly burn up the body's yin - the cooling, moistening fluids that nourish the organs. When Liver and Kidney yin are depleted, patients experience a dull, persistent ache, dry eyes, night sweats, and a red, peeled tongue.
This is why a single Western diagnosis of DILI can look so different from one person to the next. TCM identifies which pattern is dominant - damp-heat, Spleen deficiency, blood stasis, or yin deficiency - and treats accordingly. The goal is never just to lower an enzyme number, but to resolve the specific imbalance that the drug toxicity created, so the Liver can truly recover.
classical_quote: 「凡诸药毒，皆能损人脏腑，令气血逆乱，面目发黄。」
classical_translation: "All drug toxins can damage the zang-fu organs, causing disorder of Qi and Blood, and yellowing of the face and eyes."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  黄疸诸候 (Various Jaundice Syndromes) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening to the story of the drug exposure and the earliest symptoms. If the main complaints are a dull, distending ache under the ribs, poor appetite, and a sallow complexion, the picture points toward Liver Qi Stagnation with Spleen Qi Deficiency that transforms into Heat. The tongue is often pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse feels wiry and thready. A subtle bitter taste or slightly red tongue edges hints that the stagnant qi is already generating heat.
When jaundice, a bitter mouth, and dark, scanty urine dominate, the focus shifts to Liver and Gallbladder Damp-Heat. This pattern produces a red tongue with a thick, greasy yellow coating and a pulse that is rapid and wiry or slippery. The practitioner will ask about the color of the eyes and skin, because visible yellowing is a hallmark that separates damp-heat from milder qi-stagnation pictures.
If profound fatigue, heavy limbs, and loose stools overshadow the liver discomfort, the central issue is Spleen Deficiency with Dampness. Here the tongue is pale, puffy, and coated white, while the pulse is deep and weak. The practitioner distinguishes this from the mixed liver-spleen pattern by noting that distension is less pronounced than the digestive sluggishness and that heat signs like yellow tongue coat are absent.
In chronic or severe cases, a fixed, stabbing pain in the hypochondrium signals Qi And Blood Stagnation. The tongue becomes dark or purplish with possible stasis spots, and the pulse turns choppy or hesitant. The pain is not just a dull ache but a precise, piercing sensation, which helps separate blood stasis from the moving distension of qi stagnation.
When the injury has dragged on and depleted the body’s reserves, Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency emerges. Dizziness, night sweats, a dry mouth, and a red tongue with little or no coating are the clues. The pulse is thin and rapid. The practitioner rules out damp-heat because the tongue is dry rather than greasy, and the person feels more empty heat than the heavy oppression of dampness.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation with Spleen Qi Deficiency that transforms into Heat
patterns.symptoms: ["Distending or wandering rib pain that worsens with stress", "Abdominal bloating and loose stools after eating", "Irritability, quick temper, or frequent sighing", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Fatigue and low energy", "Sensation of heat in the chest or face"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress, anger, or frustration, Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Alcohol, Overwork, insufficient rest, or late nights
patterns.better_with: Gentle movement or walking, Light, easily digested meals, Rest, relaxation, and emotional calm
patterns.why_this_happens: Drug toxins first injure the Liver, blocking the smooth flow of Qi. That stuck Qi creates a bloated, distending sensation under the ribs and makes you irritable. At the same time, the toxins weaken the Spleen's ability to transform food and fluids, leading to loose stools and fatigue. The prolonged Qi stagnation then generates Heat, which rises to cause a bitter taste and a sensation of warmth in the chest or face.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, teeth marks, thin-to-moderately thick yellow and slightly greasy coating. Pulse: wiry and rapid, especially taut in the left Guan (Liver) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional frustration directly stagnates Liver Qi, which is the root of this pattern, while greasy, spicy, or alcoholic substances generate Damp-Heat and further burden the already weakened Spleen. Light meals and gentle movement ease the digestive load and encourage Qi to flow smoothly, preventing the buildup of pressure and Heat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Favour easily digested, lightly cooked foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and small amounts of lean protein. Avoid alcohol, coffee, deep-fried and spicy foods, which add more Heat and dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking or stretching helps Qi flow, and a short rest after meals supports the Spleen.

patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with red sides and a thick, yellow, greasy coating. Pulse: wiry, slippery, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy, and rich foods directly generate more dampness and heat, feeding the root of this pattern, while alcohol is a hot toxin that further damages the Liver. Rest allows the body to redirect energy toward healing, and avoiding emotional stress prevents additional Liver Qi stagnation that would trap damp-heat even more.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, easily digestible meals with plenty of leafy greens and vegetables. Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and rich foods completely. Bitter greens like dandelion and teas made from corn silk can gently drain damp-heat. Rest is essential-overwork and alcohol will worsen the condition. Drink enough water to help flush toxins, but avoid ice-cold drinks which can hinder digestion.

patterns.why_this_happens: Many medications are inherently toxic and can weaken the Spleen's ability to transform and transport fluids and food. When Spleen Qi is compromised, dampness accumulates internally because the body's metabolic engine is too sluggish to manage moisture. This dampness then sinks downward, producing loose stools, and settles into the limbs, causing a heavy, leaden sensation. The resulting fatigue and poor appetite reflect the Spleen's failure to extract and distribute nourishment from food, a classic consequence of drug-induced injury to the middle burner.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks and a white, greasy coating. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slow (Huan), soft and lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on warmth and moderate activity. Cold and raw foods douse its digestive fire, while greasy foods create more dampness. Gentle movement and warm, simple meals support the Spleen's transport function, helping to dry out accumulated dampness and restore normal energy production.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Emphasize warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and small amounts of ginger. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that further burden the Spleen. Gentle daily movement such as walking helps Qi move and dampness resolve, but avoid overexertion.

patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a taut guitar string scraping bamboo.

Greasy foods and overwork further clog the Liver's filtering function. Gentle movement and warmth encourage Qi and Blood to flow, breaking up the stagnation and easing the fixed pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep meals light and avoid greasy, fried, or overly rich foods that can burden the Liver. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps keep Qi and Blood flowing. Applying a warm compress over the right rib area can temporarily ease the stabbing sensation.

patterns.why_this_happens: Drug toxicity is a form of heat that, over time, burns up the body's yin fluids. The Liver stores blood and the Kidneys store essence; when yin is depleted, the Liver loses its moistening and the Kidneys fail to anchor yang. This produces the dull, persistent hypochondriac ache, dry eyes, and lower back soreness typical of this pattern. The empty heat that arises from yin deficiency then further irritates the liver and disturbs sleep, creating a cycle of damage and depletion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine (thin, thread-like) and rapid, often slightly wiry; weak at the left chi (Kidney) and left guan (Liver) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling, moistening resource. Rest and nourishing foods replenish it, while overwork, heat, and stimulants burn it up. When yin is depleted, empty heat rises, further damaging the liver and disturbing sleep. By protecting and rebuilding yin, the liver regains its ability to function smoothly and the hypochondriac pain and dryness subside.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, tofu, cucumber, and goji berries. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods that consume yin. Prioritize rest, especially before midnight, and avoid overwork and late-night screen time. Gentle exercise like tai chi or walking supports qi flow without depleting fluids.

faqs.question: Can TCM help my liver heal after a medication injury?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be an excellent support during recovery. Herbal formulas and acupuncture are tailored to your specific pattern - whether that means clearing damp-heat, strengthening the Spleen, or nourishing depleted yin. Many patients report improved energy, better digestion, and a gradual normalization of liver enzymes within weeks of starting treatment. However, it's critical that the offending drug has already been stopped under medical supervision; TCM supports healing but cannot reverse ongoing toxic exposure.

faqs.question: Is it safe to take Chinese herbs if my liver was damaged by a drug?
faqs.answer: When prescribed by a qualified TCM practitioner, the herbs used for DILI are specifically chosen for their liver-protective and restorative properties. Classic formulas like Yin Chen Hao Tang or Yi Guan Jian have been used safely for centuries to treat liver conditions. That said, some herbs can be hepatotoxic in the wrong context, which is why self-prescribing is dangerous - especially for a liver already under stress. Always inform your practitioner of every medication and supplement you take, and work with someone experienced in managing liver conditions.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results?
faqs.answer: Many patients notice an improvement in symptoms like fatigue, nausea, and rib discomfort within the first 2-3 weeks. Liver enzyme levels may take longer to reflect the healing, often 4-8 weeks. The timeline depends on the severity of the injury and your pattern type - excess conditions like damp-heat tend to clear faster, while deficiency patterns require more time to rebuild the body's reserves. Consistency with herbs and weekly acupuncture sessions is key.

faqs.question: What should I eat during recovery?
faqs.answer: Focus on light, easily digested foods that don't overburden the Liver and Spleen. Cooked vegetables, congee, and soups are ideal. Favor cooling, moistening foods like pear, cucumber, tofu, and leafy greens, especially if you have signs of heat or yin deficiency. Bitter greens and dandelion tea can gently support the Liver. Avoid greasy, fried, or spicy foods, alcohol, and large, heavy meals - these create more dampness and heat that the Liver must process. Ginger tea can be helpful if your digestion feels sluggish and you tend toward loose stools.

faqs.question: Can I continue my other medications while doing TCM?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. TCM is used alongside necessary conventional medications, not as a replacement. However, you must inform both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor about everything you are taking. Some herbs can interact with pharmaceuticals, particularly those metabolized by the liver. Your practitioner will choose formulas that support liver function without adding burden, and your doctor can monitor for any interactions. Never stop a prescribed medication without your doctor's guidance.

faqs.question: Will acupuncture help?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can be a valuable part of treatment, especially for relieving rib pain, reducing stress, and supporting digestive function. Points like Taichong (LR-3) and Yanglingquan (GB-34) help move stagnant Liver Qi, while Zusanli (ST-36) strengthens the Spleen. For many patients, weekly sessions provide noticeable symptom relief and a sense of calm that supports overall healing. Acupuncture alone is rarely sufficient for significant liver injury - it works best in combination with herbal medicine.

research.description: This expert consensus provides TCM pattern differentiation and treatment protocols for drug-induced liver injury in HIV/AIDS patients, emphasizing the use of formulas like Yin Chen Hao Tang for damp-heat and Shen Ling Bai Zhu San for spleen deficiency.
